title: Indiaspora Names Kiran Ghia an Inspiring Icon for STEM Work in Rural Mississippi
excerpt: As Chief Strategy Advisor at the Global Teaching Project, the Indian American advocate has helped bring free AP STEM classes to more than 4,000 students in over 50 rural Mississippi schools over the past decade.
body:
• Indiaspora, the nonprofit network of global leaders of Indian descent, has named Indian American education advocate Kiran Ghia an Inspiring Icon for bringing free Advanced Placement STEM classes to rural Mississippi schools.
  • Ghia is Chief Strategy Advisor at the Global Teaching Project (GTP), which over the past ten years has worked with more than 50 schools and served over 4,000 rural Mississippi students, according to Indiaspora.
  • GTP offers AP Physics, AP Biology, AP Statistics and AP Computer Science Principles in a blended format, and supplies laptops, lab equipment and textbooks. All of its programming is free to students, schools and families.
  • Ghia's newest project is a documentary short, now in pre-production, about the Indian teachers who have come to Mississippi's Delta region over the last 20 years.

Indiaspora has named Kiran Ghia, an Indian American lawyer turned education advocate, one of its Inspiring Icons, recognizing a decade of work bringing free Advanced Placement STEM courses to high school students in rural Mississippi who would otherwise have no access to them. Announcing the selection, Indiaspora said Ghia's story reflects what it celebrates in the diaspora: "children of immigrants who carry forward the values of their families by investing in the communities where they live, one corner of the world at a time."

Ghia is Chief Strategy Advisor at the Global Teaching Project (GTP). Her work takes her to the Mississippi Delta and other rural parts of the state, where access to advanced high school coursework, particularly in STEM, is severely limited, and where schools face a chronic and worsening shortage of qualified teachers, Indiaspora said.

The work in Mississippi

GTP provides promising high school students in rural, high-poverty Mississippi communities with access to the advanced STEM courses their schools may not be able to offer. It works with faculty and students from Yale, the University of Virginia, Harvard, Notre Dame, Delta State, Jackson State, Ole Miss and Mississippi State, among other universities, to offer AP Physics, AP Biology, AP Statistics and AP Computer Science Principles in a blended format. GTP also supplies laptops, lab equipment and textbooks so students can engage fully in the courses.

https://www.instagram.com/p/Df2T25jm48J/

Over the past ten years, GTP has worked with more than 50 schools and served over 4,000 rural Mississippi students — a deliberately select group, many of them in the top 10 percent of their class, who are likely to become future leaders of their communities, according to Indiaspora. All of GTP's programming is free to students, schools and families, and the program is currently funded entirely by private support.

Ghia describes the model as built to sustain itself. She points to one student from a school deep in the Delta who took AP Physics through GTP, passed the exam and went on to Mississippi State University: "He graduated from Mississippi State and he's now back teaching AP Physics at Leflore High School, the same high school he once attended… this is how you do it. This is how it works, and this is how you can see a self-sustaining future."

"We have an obligation, a moral obligation, and a duty to ensure that all of our children, not just in the Delta, not just in the cities, but all over the country have access to opportunity and have access to an education."

— Kiran Ghia, Chief Strategy Advisor, Global Teaching Project

From a professors' household to the Delta

Both of Ghia's parents, Dr. Kirti Ghia and Dr. Urmila Ghia, came to the United States in the 1960s as young immigrants from India and became university professors at the University of Cincinnati — her mother in mechanical engineering and her father in aerospace engineering. "For Kiran, a child of immigrants from India, the work is rooted in the values her professor parents instilled in her, and in a belief that we must start where the need is greatest, even in a small corner of the world," Indiaspora said.

Ghia is originally a lawyer by training. She graduated from Yale College magna cum laude with distinction in History and holds a JD from Georgetown University Law Center, according to her Global Teaching Project biography. She began her career as a law clerk to U.S. District Judge Reginald C. Lindsay of the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts, practiced international and human rights law at a major international law firm, and served as Director and inaugural CEO of The Leadership Foundation of India, which promotes educational opportunity for girls and supports Avasara Academy, a secondary school and leadership academy for adolescent girls in India.

Telling the story of the Delta's Indian teachers

Ghia's newest project is a documentary short about the Indian teachers who have come to the Delta over the last 20 years. Rural Mississippi schools, facing teacher shortages, have recruited teachers from India to fill the gap; walking down the science corridor of majority Black schools, Ghia would see one Indian teacher after another, from Delhi, Hyderabad and beyond. She began developing the film with Christina MacGillivray, a filmmaker who spent over a decade in India, and it is now in pre-production. "I want so badly for our community to know what our own people are doing," Ghia said.

Ghia credits GTP's founder and CEO, Matt Dolan, for reshaping her perspective on service: "We must start where the need is the greatest. Even if it's a small corner of the world. Even if it's hard."

Schools and families can learn more through the Global Teaching Project; its courses are free to those it serves.
